title: ES words are exactly Frobenius numbers of glued semigroups ⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩
connection: Johnson/Brauer–Shockley gluing gives g(⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩) = t·g(u,v) + (t−1)(u+v) = tuv − u − v when gcd(u,v) = gcd(t,u+v) = 1 (checked by brute force on 488 triples, scripts/z52b_signature_frob_check.py). So (★)/word-form ES (F16) ⟺ every hard prime p is the Frobenius number of a 3-generated numerical semigroup ⟨4Cu, 4CB, u+B⟩; for (★) words gcd(4C, u+B) = gcd(4C, p) = 1 automatically.
why: Rosales–García-Sánchez–García-García–Jiménez Madrid proved every positive integer is the Frobenius number of SOME 3-generated semigroup: ES becomes a restriction of a solved universality theorem to a structured sub-family (complete intersections glued from a 2-generated piece).
first_step: Read Rosales et al. (Math. Scand. 94 (2004) 5–12): which 3-generator family does their construction use for odd g, and can it be forced into the shape ⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩ with 4 | t?

title: Symmetric 3-generated semigroups = complete intersections (Herzog): ES as a symmetric-Frobenius representation problem
connection: Herzog: 3-generated symmetric numerical semigroups are complete intersections, i.e. gluings ⟨d·a, d·b, c⟩ with c ∈ ⟨a,b⟩, gcd(d,c) = 1, whose Frobenius numbers are d(ab − a − b) + (d − 1)c. ES words are the slice c = a + b; other c = αa + βb give other trilinear words dab − a(d − (d−1)α) − b(d − (d−1)β).
why: Gives a natural ambient family (all symmetric 3-generated Frobenius numbers = all odd numbers?) containing the ES words; the question 'which (α,β) slices are universal on primes' is a clean ladder of problems, some maybe solved.
first_step: Enumerate, for odd n ≤ 10⁶, which (α,β) ∈ {0,1,2}² slices of d(ab−a−b)+(d−1)(αa+βb) with 4 | d represent n; compare failure sets with U(n)/T1.
refs: unverified: Herzog 1970, Generators and relations of abelian semigroups and semigroup rings (manuscripta math.)

title: Rødseth/Greenberg 3-generator Frobenius algorithm vs. ES₅ continued-fraction length
connection: The Rødseth algorithm computes g(a,b,c) via a negative-continued-fraction (Euclid) expansion of a ratio mod a; for ⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩ that expansion is short. Compare with λ(p) ≤ 3 (F17).
why: If the Rødseth expansion of the glued semigroup is exactly the length-3 negative CF of the ES₅ form, the semigroup literature (Kannan, Ramírez Alfonsín) becomes a dictionary for ES₅.
first_step: Run Rødseth's algorithm symbolically on ⟨tu, tv, u+v⟩ and record the CF; check against the BOARD2_SLATE ES₅ slice definitions.
refs: unverified: Rødseth 1978, On a linear diophantine problem of Frobenius (J. reine angew. Math.)

title: Feature flip: Frobenius numbers of 2-generated semigroups are exactly the t = 1 words (uv − u − v)
connection: g(u,v) = uv − u − v; n is such a number iff n + 1 = (u−1)(v−1)·… i.e. iff n+1 has a suitable factorisation — the t = 1 analogue of ES is a primality-type condition on n+1 (fails at n+1 prime). ES flips t from 1 to a multiple of 4 and gains the third generator u+v.
why: Shows precisely which feature (the third, glued generator) converts a primality obstruction into a plausible universality statement.
first_step: Tabulate which odd n fail to be g(⟨tu,tv,u+v⟩) for t = 1,2,3,4 separately (each t has its own primality-type failure set) and the union.

title: Genus/Sylvester count of the ES semigroup as a second invariant attached to each witness
connection: Each ES witness (t,u,v) gives a symmetric semigroup S with genus (gaps) (g+1)/2 = (p+1)/2 and an Apéry set of size min generator; these invariants are fixed by p, so ES asks for a semigroup with prescribed Frobenius number and prescribed shape.
why: Counting numerical semigroups by genus is a mature field (Kaplan, Zhai's Fibonacci-like growth); ES asks for one member of a structured subclass among ~φ^g semigroups of genus g — a sparse-subfamily existence question.
first_step: Check OEIS/semigroup tables (e.g. GAP package numericalsgps) for counts of complete-intersection semigroups with given Frobenius number.
refs: unverified: Zhai 2013, Fibonacci-like growth of numerical semigroups of a given genus (Semigroup Forum)

title: xy + yz + zx: at most 19 non-represented integers (Borwein–Choi) — a solved sibling with the same symmetric form
connection: n ≠ xy+yz+zx (x,y,z ≥ 1) for 18 known n and at most one more (none under GRH). ES's surface is 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx): the same symmetric quadratic σ₂ appears. Shares F01, F14, F25 (explicit finite exception list), F23.
why: The proof route (class numbers of −4n-type discriminants, Weinberger's idoneal bound, ineffectivity via Siegel) is a template for 'all but at most one' pointwise results — an outcome shape ES has never had.
first_step: Read Borwein–Choi (Exp. Math. 9 (2000)) and identify how r_{σ₂}(n) is written as a class-number sum; look for an analogous expression of the ES count on the slice σ₂ = 4σ₃/n.

title: Restrict ES to its σ₂-level sets: (x,y,z) with xy+yz+zx = M and xyz = nM/4
connection: Every ES solution lies on a pair of level sets of elementary symmetric functions σ₂ = M, σ₃ = nM/4; for each M, (x,y,z) are roots of T³ − σ₁T² + MT − nM/4.
why: Turns ES into: find M and σ₁ such that a cubic with these coefficients splits over ℤ with positive roots — a 'split cubic' problem like those handled by discriminant/class-group methods.
first_step: For hard primes p ≤ 10⁶ list the M = σ₂ values of all solutions; look for structure (e.g. M ≡ 0 mod p, M/p values) suggesting a 1-parameter family.

title: Weinberger 'at most one exception' via Siegel–Tatuzawa: target theorem shape for ES
connection: Weinberger showed at most one further idoneal number exists (ineffective). Tatuzawa: L(1,χ_D) ≫_ε D^{−ε} for all D but at most one.
why: A realistic intermediate goal for ES: 'ES holds for all primes except possibly those attached to a single exceptional real character'. ES's BM main term is a sum of Kronecker characters χ_{−4uB}(p) (F20), exactly where a Siegel-type dichotomy acts.
first_step: Check whether the Burgess input in Thm 2.2 (M_BM(p) ≥ 0.019 log²p) can be replaced by Siegel–Tatuzawa to get a larger constant for all p outside one exceptional modulus.
refs: unverified: Weinberger 1973, Exponents of the class groups of complex quadratic fields (Acta Arith.)
unverified: Tatuzawa 1951, On a theorem of Siegel (Japan. J. Math.)

title: Deuring–Heilbronn / Heath-Brown 'twin primes from Siegel zeros' as a conditional route for ES
connection: Heath-Brown showed that existence of Siegel zeros implies infinitely many twin primes (Siegel zero breaks the parity barrier). ES's obstruction is parity-like (F22) and its main term is a sum of real characters.
why: A 'Siegel zero ⇒ ES' or 'Siegel zero ⇒ ES for all large p' theorem would be a genuine new conditional result, and the dichotomy (no Siegel zero ⇒ better Burgess-type bounds) is the standard way to get unconditional pointwise statements.
first_step: Assume χ_D exceptional (χ_D(ℓ) = −1 for most small ℓ); compute whether 4Cp+1 then tends to have many divisors in −1 mod 4C (model with random primes conditioned on χ_D(ℓ) = −1).
refs: unverified: Heath-Brown 1983, Prime twins and Siegel zeros (Proc. LMS 47)

title: Euler–Goldbach: 4xy − x − y is never a square — T1 at level t = 4 is an 18th-century theorem
connection: The classical result (z² = 4xy − x − y has no positive solutions; MathOverflow 364853 traces origin and variations) is exactly the C = 1 case of T1 (D⁻₄(4m²+1) = 0). Shares F08 (square obstruction by reciprocity), F16.
why: The MO thread collects variations (other coefficients, more variables); each proved variation is a candidate new T1-type certificate or a candidate NON-obstruction, which is what ES needs at non-square n.
first_step: Read MO 364853 and its references; list every proved variant 'k·xy − x − y ≠ f(z)' and test which correspond to ES slices.

title: IMO 2007/5 Vieta jumping (4ab−1 | (4a²−1)² ⇒ a = b) as an involution proof of T1-type statements
connection: The IMO problem is the same form 4ab − 1 as level-4 ES divisors (d ≡ −1 mod 4). Its standard solution is Vieta jumping (infinite descent on an involution orbit).
why: Vieta-jumping proofs give a dynamical (descent) proof of non-existence; reversing them (ascent) is a way to generate witnesses — F38.
first_step: Write the Vieta involution on ES words p = 4uBC − u − B in u (fixing B, C) and check whether it maps solutions of p to solutions of related n.

title: Apollonian local-global is FALSE by quadratic/quartic reciprocity (Haag–Kertzer–Rickards–Stange) ↔ T1
connection: HKRS prove entire quadratic and quartic families of curvatures are missed in many integral Apollonian packings despite no congruence obstruction (Annals 200 (2024)). Same signature as T1: local conditions fine, reciprocity kills square-type families (F06, F08).
why: Their refined conjecture ('local + reciprocity obstructions are the only ones') is the precise analogue of 'U(n) fails only at squares + finite set'; the quartic part suggests looking for quartic-reciprocity obstructions in ES sub-families.
first_step: Read HKRS §§3–5 (the invariant they attach to the orbit) and attempt to define the same invariant on the ES forest / word set; test on n = 2m², n = −m² mod ℓ slices.

title: Shi (2026): local-global also false for generalized circle packings — more reciprocity-obstruction templates
connection: Extension of HKRS to four further packing types (J. Number Theory 2026). Each new packing type is a new data point for 'which orbit structures admit reciprocity obstructions'.
why: A classification of when reciprocity obstructions arise could decide whether ES-type word sets beyond Type I/II can carry them.
first_step: Check whether Shi gives a general criterion (e.g. existence of a quadratic form invariant mod squares along the orbit).

title: Lenstra: ≤ 11 divisors of N in a class r mod s when s > N^{1/3} — a uniform upper bound per ES level
connection: For N = 4Cp + 1 and s = 4C, Lenstra's bound applies when 4C ≳ p^{1/2}, giving O(1) witnesses per such level; algorithmically (Coppersmith–Howgrave-Graham–Nagaraj) they are found in poly time. Shares F10.
why: Gives an unconditional per-level cap; but note that for large C the witnesses are just small (u,B) with uB ≤ √p — a useful sanity link between the divisor and word pictures.
first_step: Verify the dictionary: d = 4Cu − 1, d' = 4CB − 1 ⇒ (4Cu−1)(4CB−1) = 4Cp + 1 ⟺ p = 4uBC − u − B; tabulate R(p) split by C ≤ √p vs C > √p.

title: Coppersmith lattice method to sample ES witnesses at C ≈ p^{1/4}–p^{1/2}
connection: Coppersmith–Howgrave-Graham–Nagaraj find divisors in a residue class for s > N^{1/4} (with more work). For ES levels C in [p^{1/4}, p^{1/2}] this is a non-brute-force witness finder.
why: Turns the search into a lattice-reduction problem; lattice structure could expose WHY witnesses exist (short vectors) — F31.
first_step: Implement the Lenstra/Coppersmith divisor search for N = 4Cp+1, r = −1, s = 4C at C ≈ p^{0.3}, p = 10¹⁵ primes; count hits vs. expectation.
refs: unverified: Coppersmith, Howgrave-Graham, Nagaraj 2008, Divisors in residue classes, constructively (Math. Comp.)

title: Ford-style 'anatomy' model: which levels C can host a witness
connection: A random N with k = ω(N) prime factors has ≤ 2^k divisors; their residues mod 4C hit the class −1 with probability ≈ 1 − exp(−2^k/φ(4C)). With ω ≈ log log p, only levels C ≲ (log p)^{log 2} are 'likely' — an anatomy prediction for where ES witnesses live (cf. Ford's H(x,y,2y)).
why: Ford solved the divisor-in-interval problem via the anatomy of prime factors; the analogous divisor-in-class statistic would give a sharp prediction for the distribution of the smallest working level.
first_step: Compute, for hard primes p ≤ 10⁹, the smallest C with a (★) witness and compare its distribution with (log p)^{log 2}; regress on ω(4Cp+1).
refs: unverified: Ford 2008, The distribution of integers with a divisor in a given interval (Annals 168)

title: Maier–Tenenbaum propinquity of divisors as a divisor-structure template
connection: Erdős conjectured almost all n have divisors d < d' ≤ 2d; Maier–Tenenbaum proved it. ES needs 'divisor in a coset of a subgroup' rather than 'two divisors close'. Shares F10w, F05 (almost all).
why: The Maier–Tenenbaum argument controls the joint distribution of log-divisors; a residue-class version would be the multiplicative-group analogue.
first_step: Check whether a residue-class analogue of Maier–Tenenbaum ('almost all N have a divisor ≡ −1 mod q for q ≤ (log N)^c') is in the literature.
refs: unverified: Maier, Tenenbaum 1984, On the set of divisors of an integer (Invent. Math.)

title: Cramér's conjecture as the closest 'polylog-many expected events must not all fail' analogue
connection: Cramér: every interval [x, x + C log²x] contains a prime — expected count ≍ log x, pointwise, unprovable. ES: ≍ log²p expected witnesses at each prime. Shares F04, F21, F24, F23 (prime gaps verified to 2⁶⁴).
why: Whatever makes Cramér hopeless (no structure at polylog scale) is a diagnostic: ES must use structure Cramér lacks (fixed-p algebra, BM-exact main term) or it is equally hopeless.
first_step: Write a one-paragraph 'what ES has that Cramér lacks' list and check each item against the existing proof attempts.

title: Maier's matrix method for ES: build primes where the Poisson model under-predicts failures
connection: Maier showed the Cramér model fails in short intervals because small-prime biases correlate events. For ES, choose p in progressions modulo products of small primes (p a square mod many ℓ) and measure R(p) relative to M_BM(p).
why: If R(p)/M_BM(p) is systematically smaller on such 'Maier primes', the one-sided H⁻_BM is at risk; if not, it is evidence the BM normalisation already absorbs the Maier effect.
first_step: Take primes p ≡ 1 mod 840·∏ℓ with p a QR mod every ℓ ≤ 50, p ≈ 10¹²; compute R(p)/M_BM(p) vs. random primes of same size.

title: Granville's corrected Cramér model ↔ BM-corrected Poisson model for R(p)
connection: Granville refined Cramér's model by sieving small primes, predicting larger gaps (ξ ≥ 2e^{−γ}). ES's analogue is replacing the naive density 1/(4uC−1) by 1/φ and then by the BM-corrected main term.
why: A precise 'Granville-type' ES model would predict the maximal size of log P(R = 0 | M) and hence whether finitely many failures are expected.
first_step: Fit P(R*(n) = 0 | M_BM(n)) on odd non-squares ≤ 10⁸ against e^{−cM} with c from a sieved Poisson model.
refs: unverified: Granville 1995, Harald Cramér and the distribution of prime numbers (Scand. Actuarial J.)

title: Legendre / Oppermann (prime between consecutive squares): almost-all known, pointwise open — another polylog-to-polynomial sibling
connection: Prime in (n², (n+1)²): count ≍ n/log n, almost-all via zero-density, pointwise open. Shares F01, F05, F21, F23. Feature flip vs ES: count polynomial rather than polylog (larger budget, still open).
why: Calibration: a method that would prove ES pointwise but not Legendre must use something specific to ES's algebra.
first_step: List which ES pointwise programs (H⁻_BM etc.) would, if transplanted, also prove Legendre — those are suspect.

title: Least quadratic non-residue: exists iff n is not a square — the exact reciprocity shape of T1
connection: For n > 1, some prime ℓ has (n/ℓ) = −1 iff n is not a square; the least one is ≪ log²n under GRH (Ankeny/Bach) and ≪ n^{1/(4√e)+ε} unconditionally. ES's BM layer is pointwise free iff n is not a square (SYNTHESIS_SPARKS9 Prop 2.2).
why: This is the only fully solved problem whose failure set is exactly the squares; ES's remaining difficulty is the 'one more character' step beyond it.
first_step: Quantify: for hard primes ≤ 10⁹ correlate ℓ(p) (least non-residue) with R(p) and with the smallest working level; check whether R(p) is small exactly when ℓ(p) is large.

title: Artin's conjecture: quantifier flip (∃a ∀∞p) vs ES (∀p ∃ witness); Heath-Brown 'one of three' shape
connection: Heath-Brown (Quart. J. Math. 37 (1986)): among any three multiplicatively independent candidates, at most two fail to be primitive roots for infinitely many p. Squares can never be primitive roots (F08-like obstruction). Shares F08w, F22 (Chen/Fouvry–Iwaniec sieve).
why: The quantifier order is flipped, which is instructive: fixed-witness/varying-p statements are sieve-accessible; ES's ∀p∃ needs the opposite.
first_step: Formulate the ES analogue 'for any three fixed (u,B) pairs, at most two lines fail for a positive proportion of p' — check it is trivial or false.

title: Least primitive root ≪ p^{1/4+ε} (Burgess) as a pointwise-small-witness template
connection: Pointwise existence of a small witness (primitive root) with the bound coming from character-sum estimates (Burgess) — same input as ES's M_BM ≥ 0.019 log²p bound.
why: Shows the Burgess route gives pointwise statements only when ONE character sum controls the event; ES needs control of many characters mod 4uB simultaneously.
first_step: Write the ES (★) event at fixed level as a sum over characters mod 4uB and identify the minimal set whose Burgess control suffices for one (u,B).

title: Linnik's n = p + x² + y² (dispersion method): pointwise count of a divisor-character sum along a long family
connection: r₂(n − p) = 4Σ_{d|n−p} χ₋₄(d): Linnik proved Σ_p r₂(n−p) ∼ main term for every large n. ES's R(p) = Σ_C D_{4C}⁻(4Cp+1) is also a sum over a family of divisor-in-class counts (F10, F20, F21).
why: Difference to pin down: Linnik's family has length ≍ n (huge mean), ES's effective length is log p (polylog mean) — the dispersion method needs the long family; quantify how long an ES family would need to be.
first_step: Compute the variance of D_{4C}⁻(4Cp+1) over C ≤ X for fixed p, X = p^θ; see at which θ a dispersion bound would give R > 0.
refs: unverified: Linnik 1960, An asymptotic formula in an additive problem of Hardy–Littlewood (Izv.)

title: Hooley's GRH proof of p + x² + y² before Linnik: GRH sufficed there — why not for ES?
connection: Hooley (1957) proved the Hardy–Littlewood p + x² + y² asymptotic under GRH; Linnik later removed GRH. For ES, GRH is not known to imply anything pointwise (F36).
why: The precise reason (length of averaging) gives a sharp test for any proposed 'GRH ⇒ ES' argument.
first_step: Re-derive in one page where Hooley uses the length-n average over p and write the ES analogue with length log p.
refs: unverified: Hooley 1957, On the representation of a number as the sum of two squares and a prime (Acta Math.)

title: Hooley's τ(n² + a) asymptotics ↔ Type I divisors of p² + 4c²d
connection: Type I ES ⟺ f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p (mod 4cd): divisors of a quadratic polynomial value in a residue class. Hooley's method (equidistribution of roots of quadratic congruences; Duke–Friedlander–Iwaniec) controls Σ_n τ(n² + a).
why: For ES one varies (c,d) at fixed p — the family is the polynomial's coefficients, not its argument; check if a 'coefficient-variable' Hooley theorem exists.
first_step: Search: 'divisors of n² + a in arithmetic progressions uniformly in a'; compute the Type I count vs. Hooley-type prediction at fixed p.
refs: unverified: Hooley 1963, On the number of divisors of a quadratic polynomial (Acta Math.)

title: Goldbach–Linnik: even n = p + q + K powers of 2 (K = 8, Pintz–Ruzsa) — adding a sparse structured set makes pointwise possible
connection: Linnik showed finitely many powers of 2 suffice; Heath-Brown–Puchta K = 13, Pintz–Ruzsa K = 8. Shares F01, F05 (binary Goldbach exceptional set) and the strategy 'almost-all + a sparse absorbing set'.
why: ES analogue: show 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z + (sum of K unit fractions from a sparse set S) with K bounded, then try to shrink K — a ladder of weakenings with K = ∞ trivial.
first_step: Define ES_K(S): 4/p − Σ_{i≤K} 1/s_i ∈ {1/x+1/y+1/z} for some s_i ∈ S = {2^j}; compute the least K needed for p ≤ 10⁷.
refs: unverified: Heath-Brown, Puchta 2002, Integers represented as a sum of primes and powers of two (Asian J. Math.)

title: Romanoff vs Erdős: n = p + 2^k has positive density but infinitely many failures via covering congruences
connection: Bounded expected count ⇒ covering obstruction possible (Erdős 1950). ES's expected count grows (log²p) and ES has no covering/BM obstruction (F06, F07): the flip shows exactly what protects ES.
why: If one could prove 'any obstruction to an ES-like problem with growing expected count must be a covering/BM one', ES would follow from BL — clarifies the shape of a meta-theorem.
first_step: Collect polylog-count additive problems with infinitely many failures and check whether every failure mechanism is congruential.
refs: unverified: Erdős 1950, On integers of the form 2^k + p and some related problems (Summa Brasil. Math.)

title: Crocker: infinitely many odd n ≠ p + 2^a + 2^b — polylog expected count yet infinitely many failures
connection: Expected count ≍ log n (polylog), like ES, but Crocker exhibits infinitely many exceptions. Shares F04, F24w.
why: Key calibration: a polylog expected count alone does not imply finitely many failures. Learn what structure Crocker's exceptions exploit and check that ES cannot be attacked the same way.
first_step: Check whether Crocker's exceptions come from a covering-type construction (e.g. n = 2^{2^m} − 1) and whether an ES analogue (n in a sparse algebraic family) has abnormally small R(n).
refs: unverified: Crocker 1971, On the sum of a prime and of two powers of two (Pacific J. Math.)

title: Goldbach's other conjecture (odd n = p + 2a²) fails at 5777, 5993: a finite-failure, low-count sibling
connection: Stern found the two exceptions; expected count ≍ √n/log n yet failures exist at small n. Shares F01, F25, F23.
why: Shows finite explicit exception lists arise even with growing counts; ES's analogue lists are U(n)'s {105, 2961, …} and the 14 (★) failures.
first_step: Compare the 'margin' (expected count at the exceptions) for Stern numbers with M_BM at the 14 (★) failures and at U(n) failures.

title: Ternary Goldbach (Helfgott): analytic theorem for n ≥ N₀ + computation below — the template ES would follow
connection: Helfgott: every odd n > 5 is a sum of three primes (circle method with explicit constants + verification to 8.875·10³⁰). ES has huge verification (10¹⁷–10¹⁸, F23); only the analytic half is missing.
why: Every ES proof will have this shape; knowing the verification limit sets the explicit-constant target (p₀ ≤ 10¹⁸).
first_step: Estimate what explicit constant ε in H⁻_BM would be needed for p₀ = 10¹⁸ given the proved M_BM ≥ 0.019 log²p.

title: Duke–Schulze-Pillot: ternary forms represent all large locally-represented n outside finitely many spinor square classes
connection: Spinor exceptions live on square classes tm² — the same shape as T1 (F08). Proof: Iwaniec/Duke bounds for half-integral weight cusp form coefficients; ineffective (Siegel).
why: If some ternary lattice/quaternion picture of ES (QUATERNION_ES) has T1 as its spinor-exceptional set, DSP gives 'all large non-squares' for that picture — but only if representation numbers there are ≫ n^{1/2−ε}, which ES's polylog count is not.
first_step: Locate in QUATERNION_ES which ternary form's representations map to ES witnesses; compute its theta series coefficient size at primes.

title: Ono–Soundararajan: x²+y²+10z² represents all odd n except 18 listed, under GRH
connection: A finite explicit odd exception list proved conditionally (Waldspurger + GRH-explicit L-value bounds). Shares F25 (like U(n)'s list), F23, F36w.
why: Unlike ES, GRH suffices there because the count is a weight-3/2 coefficient of size n^{1/2}; flip shows the role of the count's size.
first_step: Record the explicit constant chain in Ono–Soundararajan and compute the analogous 'margin' for ES (log² vs n^{1/2}).
refs: unverified: Ono, Soundararajan 1997, Ramanujan's ternary quadratic form (Invent. Math. 130)

title: Bhargava–Hanke 290 theorem: universality certified by a finite test set — opposite of B1
connection: A positive-definite integral form is universal iff it represents 1..290 (finite certificate). ES's B1 (F35) says no bounded procedure works for ES.
why: Feature flip: universality of ONE fixed object (escalation is finite) versus ES's ∀n∃ object; clarifies that ES lacks a finite 'escalator' structure.
first_step: Ask whether 'the set of ES word-forms tuv−u−v with t in a finite set' has an escalation theory (which finite t-sets give all large primes?).

title: Colliot-Thélène–Xu: spinor exceptions are Brauer–Manin obstructions for integral points
connection: CT–Xu (Compositio 2009) explain many integral Hasse failures for quadratic forms (spinor exceptions on square classes) as BM obstructions. ES has no BM obstruction (BL) yet T1 kills Type I/II at squares.
why: Suggests T1 is a BM obstruction on a different (sub)scheme — the Type I/II torsor — which is exactly what makes the squares special; a CT–Xu-style theorem on a non-obstructed torsor could give existence.
first_step: Identify the scheme whose integral points are Type I/II solutions and compute its Br/BM pairing at n = m² (should reproduce T1).

title: Tunnell's theorem: congruent numbers via equality of ternary theta coefficients
connection: Tunnell: n congruent ⇒ (under BSD ⇐) #{2x²+y²+8z² = n} = 2#{2x²+y²+32z² = n}. ES has an exact theta-quotient normal form (F19).
why: Shows how an existence question about rational points can be converted to a comparison of theta coefficients; ES's normal form is a difference D⁻ − D⁺ of the same kind.
first_step: Write R_t(n) = ½(D⁺+D⁻) + ½(D⁻−D⁺) − β and look for a Tunnell-type identity linking the odd part to a ternary theta series at prime n.
refs: unverified: Tunnell 1983, A classical Diophantine problem and modular forms of weight 3/2 (Invent. Math.)

title: Heegner/Monsky: every prime p ≡ 5, 7 mod 8 is congruent (resp. 2p) — ∀ primes in a class via explicit points
connection: A ∀p-in-a-class existence theorem proved by explicit construction (Heegner points / mock Heegner points). Shares F01p, F29 (residue class of p matters).
why: Template for a constructive proof that works on a residue class of primes by building a witness from an auxiliary arithmetic object (here CM points).
first_step: Search for CM / Heegner-type constructions that output divisors of 4Cp+1 in class −1 mod 4C (e.g. from ideals in ℚ(√−p) or ℚ(√−4Cp)).
refs: unverified: Monsky 1990, Mock Heegner points and congruent numbers (Math. Z.)

title: Bilu–Hanrot–Voutier primitive divisors ≡ ±1 mod n supply divisors-in-class for Lucas-type ES families
connection: Primitive prime divisors of the n-th Lucas number u_n satisfy q ≡ (D/q) mod n, and exist for all n > 30 (BHV). That is a guaranteed divisor in a class tied to the index — exactly F10 — for integers in exponential families.
why: The campaign's proved thin families (3·2^s+1, 4^s+105, …) used algebraic factorizations; BHV could give a systematic source of divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C for p-tied integers in Lucas families.
first_step: For the open families 15·2^s+1 and 4^s+297: write 4C·p+1 for small C as a Lucas-sequence value or factor thereof and check whether a primitive divisor lands in the needed class.
refs: unverified: Bilu, Hanrot, Voutier 2001, Existence of primitive divisors of Lucas and Lehmer numbers (J. reine angew. Math.)

title: Zsigmondy: finite explicit exception list via elementary cyclotomic argument
connection: a^n − b^n has a primitive prime divisor except for an explicit finite list. Shares F01, F25. Primitive divisors of a^n − 1 are ≡ 1 mod n.
why: Divisors ≡ +1 mod n come for free from cyclotomy; ES needs −1 classes — the sign flip corresponds to a^n + 1 / Lucas 'negative' sequences.
first_step: Check whether n-th primitive divisors of a^n + 1 (≡ 1 mod 2n) can be made ≡ −1 mod 4C after multiplying by known factors.

title: Graham: every n > 77 is a sum of distinct integers with reciprocals summing to 1 — inductive (n → 2n+2, 2n+9) proof
connection: Finite exceptions (F25) + all-n statement about unit fractions (F12) proved by an additive recursion. ES has only multiplicative closure (F02).
why: If an additive 'transport law' n → an + b preserving ES-solvability existed even partially, an inductive proof shape would open.
first_step: Search ES solution tables for maps (x,y,z) at n ↦ solutions at 2n+1, 4n+1 etc.; test which affine maps preserve solvability on all n ≤ 10⁵.
refs: unverified: Graham 1963, A theorem on partitions (J. Austral. Math. Soc.)

title: ES ⇒ m/n is a sum of m − 1 unit fractions for every m ≥ 4 (and 'm−1 terms' is a ladder)
connection: m/n = (m−4)·(1/n) + 4/n, so ES gives m − 1 terms. Flip: m/n in m − 2 terms is Sierpiński-type for m = 5 (3 terms) and is false for large m (Schinzel exceptions). F11, F12.
why: Places ES as the first rung of a ladder 'm/n in k(m) terms'; the threshold function k(m) is a natural object whose known values constrain methods.
first_step: Tabulate, for m ≤ 12 and n ≤ 10⁴, the least k with m/n a sum of k unit fractions; record the first m where k = m − 2 fails.

title: No diagonal ES solutions at p ≡ 1 (mod 4): the S₃ action on solutions is free
connection: If x = y then 4/p = 2/x + 1/z forces a = 2x − p ∈ {1, p²} and 4 | p + 1, so p ≡ 3 (mod 4); same for y = z. Checked: no diagonal solution for any prime p ≡ 1 (4) below 1500; parity of the unordered count is 50/50 (scripts/z52b_signature_parity.py).
why: Freeness of S₃ means the ordered count is 6× the unordered one and kills simple involution-parity proofs (Zagier-style) — a useful negative datum for F38.
first_step: Look for a non-S₃ involution (e.g. Vieta in the hyperbola fibre) whose fixed points are classifiable; count fixed points for p ≤ 10⁵.

title: Zagier's one-sentence proof (windmill involution) as the canonical parity-existence template
connection: p ≡ 1 mod 4 ⇒ sum of two squares via an involution with a unique fixed point. ES's hard primes are exactly p ≡ 1 mod 4 (F29).
why: A parity proof needs an odd count; the unordered ES count has no fixed parity (see the diagonal item) — so any windmill-type proof must count a weighted or restricted subset.
first_step: Search for a restricted ES subset (e.g. solutions with x minimal in its Vieta orbit) whose count parity is constant on hard primes ≤ 10⁵.
refs: unverified: Zagier 1990, A one-sentence proof that every prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) is a sum of two squares (Amer. Math. Monthly)

title: Vose: every m/n is a sum of O(√log n) unit fractions — bounded vs. unbounded term counts
connection: Vose's theorem gives a uniform term bound growing with n; ES fixes 3 terms (F12). Erdős conjectured O(log log n) suffices.
why: Methods that achieve O(√log n) (smooth-number denominators) might give 3 terms for numerator 4 if the smoothness budget is tuned to p.
first_step: Re-read Vose's construction and compute the number of terms it produces for 4/p, p hard, p ≤ 10⁹.
refs: unverified: Vose 1985, Egyptian fractions (Bull. London Math. Soc.)

title: Croot's coloring theorem / Bloom's density theorem: unit fractions inside dense sets
connection: Croot (Annals 2003): any finite colouring of ℕ has a monochromatic 1 = Σ1/x_i; Bloom (2021): positive upper density sets contain such sums. Shares F12, F05 (density statements).
why: Their engine (Fourier analysis over smooth numbers + combinatorics of divisors) is the strongest existing unit-fraction existence machinery; ES is the opposite extreme (3 terms, prescribed target).
first_step: Identify the step in Bloom where many terms are needed and ask if a 3-term version with target 4/p survives under a smooth-number restriction.
refs: unverified: Croot 2003, On a coloring conjecture about unit fractions (Annals 157)

title: Sierpiński 5/n: numerator flip 4 → 5 — does a T1 analogue exist for 5/n?
connection: 5/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z is open, conjectured always solvable. Shares nearly all ES features (F01, F12, F13, F05, F23); flips F11.
why: If 5/n's Type I/II analogues are NOT obstructed at squares (or are obstructed at a different set), comparing tells which part of T1 is numerator-4-specific — important for numerator-uniform-argument checks (8/131).
first_step: Define 5/n Type I/II (n divides one/two denominators) and compute whether they vanish at odd squares n = m² for m ≤ 10³.
refs: unverified: Sierpiński 1956, Sur les décompositions de nombres rationnels en fractions primaires (Mathesis)

title: Numerator flip 4 → 8: failures at 17, 131, 241 as an anti-overreach test suite
connection: 8/n has genuine exceptions (17, 131, 241 among small primes) while satisfying the same local/BM features (needs check). Any ES argument must visibly use a property false for 8.
why: Cheapest filter for candidate proofs: run them on 8/131 and 8/241.
first_step: For each tool collected in this lane, write one line: 'does the argument distinguish 4 from 8?'.

title: Schinzel's conjecture m/n three terms for n > N(m) with N(m) growing — Pomerance–Weingartner exceptions
connection: For each m, ES-type solvability is conjectured for large n, with exceptions up to exp(m^{1/3+o(1)}) (F11). ES is the m = 4 case with N(4) = 1.
why: Treat ES as the base of a family with a threshold N(m); methods that give N(m) < ∞ for one m > 4 would already be new.
first_step: Check the PW lower-bound construction for exceptions and whether its mechanism (covering by many small primes) can be run at m = 4.
refs: unverified: Pomerance, Weingartner, On primes and practical numbers / exceptions for m/n (check exact title)

title: Feature flip: allow one negative unit fraction — 4/p = 1/((p−1)/4) − 1/(p(p−1)/4) trivially
connection: Positivity (F27) is the whole difficulty: with signs, two terms suffice for p ≡ 1 mod 4. The positive cone is the 'boundary' making the surface log K3-like.
why: Suggests attacking positivity directly: start from the trivial signed solution and move inside the positive cone by symmetries of the cubic surface (Vieta moves / Cremona maps).
first_step: Enumerate signed 3-term solutions with exactly one negative term for hard p and test whether some explicit birational move lands in the positive cone.

title: Feature flip: S-integral ES (denominators in ℤ[1/ℓ]) is trivial — integrality at every prime is essential
connection: With ℓ = 2 or 3 allowed in denominators, 4/n = 3·(1/(3n/4)) or 1/n + 1/(n/3) work. Strong approximation away from S is cheap.
why: Locates the difficulty: it is the archimedean + all-finite-places integrality simultaneously (F06, F07).
first_step: For odd ℓ ≥ 5, determine the least S ∋ ℓ making ES trivial; record which S keep the problem nontrivial.

title: ES over totally real fields with totally positive denominators (e.g. ℤ[√2])
connection: Over O_K with K totally real, require x,y,z totally positive: a genuine analogue keeping positivity (F27); over imaginary fields positivity disappears and the problem trivialises.
why: A field where the analogue can be proved or disproved (units give extra room) gives a new 'proved variant' family like the F_q[T] ones (F26).
first_step: Compute, for K = ℚ(√2), totally positive prime elements π of norm ≤ 10⁴ and search for 4/π = Σ 1/x_i with x_i ≫ 0; look for failures.

title: Equal-denominator / chain sub-problems (x | y | z) as solvable slices
connection: Restricting ES to chains x | y | z or to a fixed ratio y = kx gives two-variable divisor problems with explicit criteria; the diagonal x = y is empty for p ≡ 1 mod 4 (see diagonal item).
why: Each restricted slice is a 'line' in the sense of F34; knowing exactly which primes each slice covers sharpens the infinite-covering picture.
first_step: For k = 2..20 compute which hard primes ≤ 10⁷ admit solutions with y = kx; tabulate densities.

title: Polynomial identities in Gaussian coordinates: ES solutions as polynomials in (a,b) with p = a² + b²
connection: Mordell–Schinzel forbid identities polynomial in p covering square classes (F09). Identities polynomial in (a,b) with p = a² + b² are not obviously excluded: at b = 0 they would give non-Type-I/II solutions or degenerate.
why: Hard primes are exactly p ≡ 1 mod 4 (F29) — they come with a canonical Gaussian factorisation that no p-polynomial can see.
first_step: For hard primes ≤ 10⁷ compute (a,b) and fit low-degree polynomial forms to the smallest solutions' denominators; check B1 Thm M's scope for procedures that use the two-squares decomposition.

title: Triangle altitude identity 1/r = 1/h_a + 1/h_b + 1/h_c: ES ⟸ triangle with integer altitudes and inradius n/4
connection: Any triangle has Σ1/h = s/Δ = 1/r. ES solutions whose reciprocals satisfy the triangle inequalities correspond to triangles with integral altitudes x,y,z and inradius n/4 (rational sides up to scaling).
why: Imports the classification of triangles with rational altitudes / Heronian-type parametrisations into ES; a parametrised family of such triangles with r = p/4 would be an ES family.
first_step: For hard primes ≤ 10⁵, compute the fraction of ES solutions satisfying the triangle inequality on (1/x,1/y,1/z); look up 'triangles with integer altitudes' parametrisations.

title: Descartes/Soddy: three mutually tangent circles of radii x,y,z have inner Soddy curvature 1/x+1/y+1/z + 2√((x+y+z)/xyz)
connection: ES fixes the linear part to 4/n; integrality of the Soddy curvature additionally needs (x+y+z)/(xyz) to be a rational square. Links ES to Apollonian-type curvature questions (F08 via HKRS).
why: A sub-family of ES solutions inside integral Apollonian configurations would inherit thin-orbit tools.
first_step: Count ES solutions (p ≤ 10⁵) where (x+y+z)·xyz is a square; if non-empty, look for Apollonian structure.

title: Manin–Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel prediction for integral points on the ES threefold vs. Elsholtz–Tao's N log³N
connection: The total space {4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx)} ⊂ A⁴ is a log Fano-type threefold; ET count Σ_{n≤N} f(n) ≍ N log³N (F04). CLT predict exponents from the Clemens complex of the boundary.
why: If the CLT/Wilsch framework reproduces log³ (all n) and log² (primes), the geometric picture explains which boundary strata carry solutions — a geometric handle on where witnesses live.
first_step: Compute the boundary divisor and its Clemens complex for a compactification of the ES threefold; compare max-face dimension + 1 with 3.
refs: unverified: Chambert-Loir, Tschinkel 2010, Integral points of bounded height on partial equivariant compactifications of vector groups

title: Wilsch: integral points of bounded height on a log Fano threefold — check if the ES threefold is of that type
connection: Wilsch counted integral points on a specific log Fano threefold with torus-like structure. ES's threefold is a cubic with an (S₃ × scaling) symmetry.
why: A matching asymptotic with explicit leading constant would be a cross-check on ET's log³ constant and on the BM-corrected local densities.
first_step: Check the definition of Wilsch's threefold and whether 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is birational to it or to a toric variety.
refs: unverified: Wilsch, Integral points of bounded height on a log Fano threefold (IMRN 2023?)

title: Hilbert property for integral points (Corvaja–Zannier) applied to the fibration n: X → A¹
connection: ES says the image of X(ℤ)_{>0} under n covers ℤ_{≥2}. Corvaja–Zannier relate the Hilbert property/thin images to fundamental groups. Polynomial-identity families have thin images missing squares (F09).
why: A thin-set theorem explaining why parametrised families must miss square classes would turn F09 into a geometric statement and show what a non-thin covering family must look like.
first_step: Check whether Mordell–Schinzel's impossibility is a special case of a Corvaja–Zannier-type 'images of integral points are thin' statement.
refs: unverified: Corvaja, Zannier 2017, On the Hilbert property and the fundamental group of algebraic varieties (Math. Z.)

title: Swinnerton-Dyer/Harpaz fibration method on the hyperbola fibration of the ES surface
connection: Fixing x, ES is a split hyperbola (ay − b)(az − b) = b² (F15) — integral points ↔ divisors of b² in a class. Harpaz (JEMS) handles conic log K3 surfaces by Swinnerton-Dyer's method conditionally / explicitly.
why: If ES's surface is a conic log K3 in Harpaz's sense, his explicit sufficient conditions might apply at most n.
first_step: Check Harpaz's definition (degree of the base, number of degenerate fibres, splitting) against the ES fibration in x.

title: Sums of three cubes: no BM obstruction (Colliot-Thélène–Wittenberg), log-scale counts, big computations
connection: x³+y³+z³ = n: affine cubic surface, all n ≢ ±4 mod 9 expected, BM-free, heuristic count ≍ log X up to height X, Booker–Sutherland searches. Shares F06, F07, F13, F23, F24.
why: Feature flip: there the solution set per n is infinite (search by height), ES's is finite and bounded by n^{O(1)} — which side is easier for existence proofs is informative.
first_step: Compare the singular-series/BM local density formulas: does ES's BM-corrected main term have the same shape as Heath-Brown's density for cubes?
refs: unverified: Colliot-Thélène, Wittenberg 2012, Groupe de Brauer et points entiers de deux familles de surfaces cubiques affines (Amer. J. Math.)

title: Chen's Markoff mod p theorem (nonabelian level structures): ∀p connectivity via topology of moduli of covers
connection: W. Chen proved every component of the Markoff mod-p graph has size divisible by p, completing Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak strong approximation for all large p. ∀p statement on a cubic surface proved via a non-analytic (algebro-topological) invariant.
why: A non-analytic, 'every p' theorem about a cubic surface family — exactly the kind of tool ES has never had. ES's words/forest structure (F39) may admit an analogous moduli interpretation.
first_step: Check Chen's argument structure (Annals 2024) and whether ES word sets mod q carry an action of a mapping-class-like group.
refs: unverified: William Y. Chen, Nonabelian level structures, Nielsen equivalence, and Markoff triples (Annals of Math. 2024)

title: Borwein conjecture (Chen Wang, Adv. Math. 2022): sign pattern of q-product coefficients by saddle-point + finite check
connection: ES ⟺ positivity/nonvanishing of coefficients of an explicit theta-quotient level series at prime indices (F19). Wang proved a coefficient sign pattern for all n analytically.
why: Feature flip: Wang's coefficients have an exponentially dominant main term; ES's are divisor-sized. Clarifies that an ES q-series proof needs a positivity mechanism, not asymptotics.
first_step: Look for a manifestly positive (product/sum-of-squares) expression of Σ_n R(n)q^n restricted to a progression, e.g. via Andrews-style identities.

title: Lehmer's τ(n) ≠ 0 and Serre lacunarity: coefficient non-vanishing classes
connection: Nonvanishing of q-series coefficients at every index is ES's F19 form; CM forms vanish on a structured set (inert primes), ES's level series vanish at squares (T1).
why: Serre's classification (lacunary ⟺ CM) suggests classifying q-series vanishing exactly on squares; ES's all-level series would be one.
first_step: Compute the support of Σ_{t,u,v} q^{tuv−u−v} (4|t restriction) up to 10⁸ and test whether its complement is squares ∪ finite set (U(n) data).

title: Erdős–Selfridge / Hough distortion method: positive uncovered density for 'small' covering families
connection: Hough (Annals 2015) and Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba show covering systems with large minimum modulus / Σ1/m small leave a positive density uncovered. ES's level sets {p : R_C(p) > 0} form an infinite 'covering' of primes (F34).
why: Running the distortion method on ES level sets tells which hypothesis (independence across levels? Σ density?) must fail for ES to be true.
first_step: Compute the density δ_C of primes covered by level C alone and Σ_C δ_C up to C ≤ 10³; compare with the BBMST criterion.
refs: unverified: Hough 2015, Solution of the minimum modulus problem for covering systems (Annals 181)

title: Lovász local lemma / Janson for 'avoid all levels': lower tail of R(p) as a dependency-graph problem
connection: R(p) = 0 means p avoids all level events; Janson's inequality bounds P(no event) by exp(−μ + Δ). ES needs this pointwise, but the probabilistic version gives the correct heuristic decay.
why: Already exploited in the campaign (EXSET_ARITH_JANSON); signature match with absorbing/LLL-based existence proofs in combinatorics.
first_step: Compute Δ (pair correlation of level events) for hard primes ≤ 10⁸ to see whether μ − Δ grows like log²p.

title: Shrinking-target / hitting-time for the Gauss map: λ(p) ≤ 3 as 'some orbit hits a target in ≤ 3 steps'
connection: ES₅: for each p there is q with p/q of continued-fraction length ≤ 3 (with constraints). In dynamics language: some rational point of denominator p reaches a target set within 3 Gauss-map steps.
why: Effective equidistribution of rationals with denominator p under the Gauss map (Ustinov, Bykovskii) could give counts of such q with a main term ≍ log²p.
first_step: Check Ustinov's results on the statistics of continued-fraction lengths of a/p for fixed p (number of a with length ≤ k).
refs: unverified: Ustinov, On the statistical properties of elements of continued fractions (Doklady)

title: Zaremba ↔ ES₅ duality: bounded alphabet/unbounded length vs. bounded length/unbounded alphabet
connection: Zaremba (density one: Bourgain–Kontorovich; Huang) bounds partial quotients; ES₅ bounds the length (≤ 3). Both are 'every denominator p has an a with a CF constraint' (F01, F17).
why: Bourgain–Kontorovich's thin-semigroup circle method needs Hausdorff dimension close to 1; ES₅'s length-3 set is 3-dimensional in continuant coordinates — a completely different counting regime (polylog).
first_step: Compute #{a mod p : λ(a/p) ≤ 3 with ES₅ constraints} for hard p and fit c·log²p.

title: Continuants: p = K(a,b,c) = abc + a + c (positive CF) vs ES's negative continuant tuv − u − v
connection: Length-3 continuants K(a,b,c) = abc + a + c represent every n > ? trivially (a = c = 1: b + 2), while the negative-CF version with a 4ℤ constraint is ES. The sign flip is the feature (F16, F27).
why: The positive version is trivially universal; ES lives exactly between positive and negative continuants — a mixed-sign continuant 'abc + a − c' family may interpolate.
first_step: For the 4 sign patterns of abc ± a ± c with a 4ℤ constraint on one coordinate, compute failure sets among primes ≤ 10⁷.

title: ES is a Π₁⁰ sentence (bounded witness) — like Goldbach and RH
connection: All denominators in a 3-term representation of 4/n are ≤ poly(n) (F32), so ES is ∀n ∃(bounded) — Π₁. Independence from PA/ZFC would imply truth.
why: Places ES in the Busy-Beaver/Π₁ landscape; gives the 'no counterexample is ever verifiable cheaply' meta-structure.
first_step: Write a minimal Turing machine (or Lean decidable predicate) that halts iff ES fails; compare its size with the bbchallenge Goldbach machines.

title: Is finding ES witnesses as hard as factoring p-tied integers?
connection: Witnesses ⟺ divisors of 4Cp+1 in a class (F10). Known fast heuristic (scan small C, factor small numbers). An ES-oracle reveals factors of 4Cp+1 for some C.
why: If ES witnesses are always findable in poly(log p) time by a deterministic method, that method may hide a proof; conversely, a reduction from factoring would explain why no explicit formula exists.
first_step: Measure, for p ≈ 10³⁰, the cost of the cheapest witness search (smallest C with a smooth enough 4Cp+1); check if it ever requires factoring a hard number.

title: Scholz–Brauer addition chains: ∀n statement proved on infinite thin families, open in general
connection: l(2^n − 1) ≤ n − 1 + l(n) is proved for many infinite families and verified computationally, open in general — the same 'thin families proved, no density rung' profile as ES (F30, F23).
why: Compare the family-proof techniques (Brauer chains, Hansen chains) with ES's 3·2^s + 1 family proofs; both rely on algebraic structure of 2^s.
first_step: Read Clift's computational verification and check whether the proved families cover a positive density of n.

title: Erdős–Straus over F_q[T] (proved variants) as the 'function field sibling' with the same features
connection: Polynomial analogues have proved versions (F26); the obstruction mechanisms (T1 analogue, degree/positivity substitute) can be compared exactly.
why: Where the F_q[T] proof uses a feature ES lacks (e.g. Weil bounds pointwise at a single polynomial), we learn which ingredient is missing.
first_step: List the proof ingredients of the F_q[T] theorems in FUNCTIONFIELD_ES*.md and mark each as 'available over ℤ' or not.

title: Primes p ≡ 1 mod 4 as norms: ES-hardness vs. splitting in many imaginary quadratic fields ℚ(√−uB)
connection: M_BM(p) small ⟺ χ_{−4uB}(p) = +1 for many small pairs, i.e. p splits in many ℚ(√−uB) — Chebotarev in a large compositum. Hard primes are 'maximally split' primes (F20, F29).
why: Gives an explicit adversarial family (primes totally split in the compositum of ℚ(i, √−ℓ) for ℓ ≤ L) and connects ES lower bounds to the least prime not totally split (Linnik/Lagarias–Odlyzko).
first_step: Compute R(p) for the first primes totally split in ℚ(i, √−3, √−5, √−7, √−11, …) (L up to 40) and compare with random p of same size.

title: Representation of p by x² + ny² for many n simultaneously (Cox) as a model of 'p a square mod everything small'
connection: Hard ES primes are squares modulo many small moduli (Mordell classes mod 840 are squares). Cox's theory characterises p = x² + ny² via ring class fields; the simultaneous version is a Chebotarev condition.
why: If ES-hardness is monotone in 'how many small forms represent p', one could try induction on a class-field tower.
first_step: For hard primes ≤ 10⁸ count n ≤ 100 with p = x² + ny² and correlate with R(p)/log²p.
refs: unverified: Cox, Primes of the form x² + ny² (Wiley)

title: Bourgain–Garaev sums of reciprocals in F_p: modular ES with small denominators
connection: The congruence 4·n⁻¹ ≡ x⁻¹ + y⁻¹ + z⁻¹ (mod q) with small x,y,z is a Kloosterman-type sumset problem with sharp results; the integral ES requires the exact equation.
why: Small modular solutions + a lifting step (choose q = some p-tied integer) could be a route to exact solutions; at minimum it shows which residues are reachable.
first_step: Check the Bourgain–Garaev 'sumsets of reciprocals' results and whether the ES equation mod 4Cp+1 reduces to such a sumset.
refs: unverified: Bourgain, Garaev, Sumsets of reciprocals in prime fields and multilinear Kloosterman sums (Izv. 2014)

title: Agoh–Giuga / Znám problems: unit-fraction equations with divisibility, finite solution families
connection: Znám's problem (each x_i | Π_{j≠i}x_j + 1) and Giuga numbers mix unit fractions with divisibility (F12, F10). Znám's problem solved for k ≥ 5 (Sun Qi) by construction.
why: Their constructions produce unit-fraction identities from divisor chains — a source of explicit ES-like families.
first_step: Check whether Sun Qi's construction yields 3-term identities for 4/n in any infinite family of primes.

title: Breusch/Stewart: every rational with odd denominator is a finite sum of distinct odd unit fractions
connection: Solved universal unit-fraction statement under a parity restriction; ES fixed-length with no parity constraint. Note: 4/n with all three denominators odd is impossible (parity of numerator), so ES always uses an even denominator.
why: Parity restrictions change term counts dramatically — a clean feature-flip for the 2-adic side of ES (F29).
first_step: Determine the possible 2-adic valuation patterns (v₂(x), v₂(y), v₂(z)) of ES solutions at hard primes ≤ 10⁵.

title: Odd greedy expansion termination (open): an algorithm-existence problem in unit fractions
connection: Does the odd greedy algorithm always terminate on a/b with b odd? Open, verified computationally. ES: does a natural greedy-type search always find a 3-term solution? (no — greedy gives more terms).
why: Defines an 'ES greedy' variant (choose x = ⌈p/4⌉ + k for minimal k such that the remainder is a 2-term fraction) whose success rate on hard primes is computable.
first_step: Compute min k such that 4/p − 1/(⌈p/4⌉+k) is a sum of 2 unit fractions, for hard primes ≤ 10⁹; study the distribution of k.

title: Rav / Bernstein criterion for m/n = 1/x + 1/y (divisor sums a + b ≡ 0 mod m) as the 2-term base case
connection: m/n is a sum of 2 unit fractions iff there are coprime divisors a, b of n (or of n²-related numbers) with m | a + b. ES's hyperbola fibres apply this after choosing x (F15).
why: ES = ∃x such that the 2-term criterion holds for 4/n − 1/x; a uniform version of the criterion with x as parameter is exactly the F10 divisor form.
first_step: State the criterion precisely for (4x − n)/(nx) and check equivalence with Type I/II divisor forms.
refs: unverified: Rav 1966, On the representation of rational numbers as a sum of a fixed number of unit fractions (J. reine angew. Math.)

title: Huang–Vaughan mean values for binary Egyptian fractions
connection: Counts of n ≤ N such that m/n is a sum of 2 unit fractions, and mean values of the representation counts (feature F04, F05 for the 2-term problem).
why: The 2-term problem has a fully understood exceptional set; matching its method to the ES fibration gives the 3-term exceptional set via a union over x.
first_step: Check the exact statements of Huang–Vaughan and whether their mean-value bound is uniform enough to sum over the ES parameter x.
refs: unverified: Huang, Vaughan, Mean value theorems for binary Egyptian fractions (J. Number Theory)

title: Elsholtz–Planitzer: f(n) ≥ (log n)^{log 6 + o(1)} for almost all n — the 'typical count' sibling
connection: Lower bound for the number of solutions for almost all n (F04, F05) via multiplicative structure (many prime factors ⇒ many solutions).
why: Primes have no multiplicative structure — the gap between n and p is the gap between this theorem and ES.
first_step: Check how the log 6 exponent arises and whether a 'prime-shifted' version (using factors of 4Cp+1 instead of n) gives a lower bound for most C.
refs: unverified: Elsholtz, Planitzer, The number of solutions of the Erdős–Straus equation and sums of k unit fractions (Proc. Roy. Soc. Edinburgh)

title: Absorption method (Ringel, Erdős–Faber–Lovász): approximate structure + absorber ⇒ exact
connection: Combinatorial ∀n∃ conjectures were solved by building most of the object randomly and absorbing the leftovers. ES analogue: '4/p − (a cheap unit fraction) has a 2-term decomposition' succeeds for almost all choices; the absorber is the freedom in x.
why: Forces the question: is there an 'absorbing' set of x values (depending on p only through simple data) guaranteed to contain a good one?
first_step: For hard primes ≤ 10⁸ find the minimal set X(p) of x-values (in terms of p mod small numbers) that always contains a working x; test stability.

title: Collatz (Tao 2019): almost all orbits attain almost bounded values via logarithmic density — the exceptional-set-improvement analogue
connection: ∀n conjecture (F01), almost-all known (F05), huge verification (F23), heuristic support (F24). Tao's key was changing the measure (logarithmic density) to gain an approximate invariance.
why: ES's exceptional set bound is stuck at exp(−c(log N)^{3/4}) (F40); a change of averaging measure (logarithmic weights in p, or weighting by the BM main term) might likewise gain invariance.
first_step: Recompute the ES exceptional-set argument with logarithmic density in n and see whether the 3/4 barrier changes.

title: ES as a Hurwitz-type equation with a Vieta group: orbit counts per n
connection: Hurwitz equations Σx_i² = a·Πx_i have finitely many fundamental solutions per (n,a) generating trees under Vieta moves; ES's word set has a forest structure (F39). Counting fundamental solutions vs. n is a solved problem type.
why: If ES words admit a finite 'fundamental domain' per p, existence reduces to existence of a fundamental solution with bounded size.
first_step: Define Vieta-like moves on (t,u,v) preserving tuv − u − v = p (e.g. u ↦ (something)) and compute orbit structure for p ≤ 10⁴.
refs: unverified: Hurwitz 1907, Über eine Aufgabe der unbestimmten Analysis

title: Mordell's equation for 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 1/w: complete parametrisation of the rational cubic surface
connection: The ES surface is rational; full rational parametrisations (e.g. of Σ1/x_i = 1/w) exist. Integral points of the ES fibre are thin inside the rational points (F13).
why: A parametrisation in which positivity and integrality become linear/congruence conditions could expose the T1 obstruction as a lattice condition and suggest where non-T1 solutions come from.
first_step: Write the standard parametrisation of 1/x+1/y+1/z = 1/w and substitute w = n/4; record the integrality conditions as divisibility conditions.

title: Feature flip F04: raise the expected count by allowing 4 terms with all denominators > n — does pointwise become easy?
connection: 4 terms trivial with repeats (1/n ×4); with distinct denominators all > n, the count becomes polynomial in n and circle/divisor methods apply.
why: Measures how much 'count budget' a pointwise proof needs; a descent from 4 to 3 terms (merging two unit fractions) is a classical move.
first_step: Characterise when 1/a + 1/b is a unit fraction (a = k(k+l)… form) and count 4-term solutions mergeable to 3 terms for hard p.

title: Feature flip F28: forbid Type I (p | exactly one denominator) — Type II alone fails at 14+ primes; union never fails ≤ 10⁸
connection: Restricting the type creates explicit failure sets ((★) fails at 14 primes ≤ 10¹⁰; b = 1 line at 3 primes ≤ 10¹¹); their union survives. Shares the 'two families, each with sparse failures, disjoint failure sets' structure with Heath-Brown's Artin and with Goldbach-type unions.
why: If failure sets of two families can be shown disjoint by a parity/sign argument (one fails ⇒ the other has many), ES follows for large p.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁹ the joint distribution of (R_(★)(p), R_{b=1}(p)) and test for negative correlation at small values.

title: Feature flip F02: problems without multiplicative closure (Goldbach) can't reduce to primes — ES's prime reduction as an asset
connection: ES(n) ⇐ ES(d) for d | n reduces to primes; for primes the multiplicative structure of n is gone. Conversely, composites have MORE solutions (Elsholtz–Planitzer).
why: Suggests 'prime-free' proofs: use auxiliary composites m = p·k with ES(pk) solutions having k | all denominators (equivalent to ES(p)).
first_step: For hard p, find the smallest k such that 4/(pk) has a solution with k dividing all three denominators — equals ES(p) — but study the distribution of 'near-misses' (k dividing two denominators).

title: Feature flip F06: Legendre's three squares (local obstruction 4^a(8b+7)) — what local obstruction would look like for ES
connection: Three-squares fails exactly on a locally-defined set; ES has none (F06). Where local obstructions are absent, ternary problems were solved via class numbers (Gauss).
why: Provides the contrast: ES's exceptional behaviour (T1 at squares) is not local but reciprocity-based, like spinor exceptions (DSP item).
first_step: Write the ES local densities at 2 and at p and confirm they never vanish at hard primes (sanity check for BL).

title: Feature flip F21: problems where a pointwise bound came from averaging over an auxiliary parameter of length ≫ polylog
connection: Pointwise results (Linnik p + x² + y², Vinogradov three primes, Duke ternary) all average over an auxiliary variable of polynomial length. ES's auxiliary variables (C, u, B) have polynomial range but polylog effective mass.
why: Suggests looking for an ES formulation with an auxiliary average of polynomial MASS (e.g. counting weighted solutions with weights growing in C).
first_step: Search for a weighting w(C,u,B) with Σ w·1[event] provably positive and mass ≫ p^δ — e.g. weights from smooth-number counts.

title: Feature flip F17: CF length ≤ 2 — which primes are length-2 (two-term) representable — fully explicit
connection: λ(p) ≤ 2 corresponds to 2-term-type representations, characterised by divisor conditions (Rav). ES₅ is the length-3 rung.
why: Explicit rung below ES; the step 2 → 3 adds one free parameter, which is where the log² count appears.
first_step: Compute the density of primes with λ(p) ≤ 2 (under ES₅ constraints) — should decay like a power of 1/log.

title: Feature flip F20: if only real characters contributed (pure genus count), ES would follow from genus theory
connection: R*(n) = M_gen(n) + X(n); M_gen is genus (order ≤ 2 characters), X the rest. Problems where only genus characters appear (class number one, idoneal discriminants) are solved by genus theory.
why: Idoneal-type phenomena: when the class group is 2-torsion, representation = genus condition. ES-hardness at a prime could be measured by how far relevant class groups are from being 2-torsion.
first_step: For hard primes, compute X(p)/M_gen(p) and correlate with the 2-rank vs. size of class groups of ℚ(√−p·small).

title: Feature flip F37: one-sided statements — 'R(p) ≥ ε·M(p)' vs. two-sided — examples of proved one-sided lower bounds
connection: Two-sided asymptotics are false for R(p) (Linnik-type large values). Proved one-sided lower bounds of the right order exist for e.g. Σ_{n ≤ x} λ-type sieve problems (Chen) but not pointwise for polylog counts.
why: Collecting proved one-sided pointwise lower bounds (any field) for counts of polylog size would show whether any precedent exists at all.
first_step: Literature search: 'pointwise lower bound' 'representation number' 'log' — look for any theorem giving r(n) ≫ (log n)^c for all n in a natural problem.

title: Precedent search: theorems giving r(n) ≫ (log n)^c for ALL n (polylog pointwise lower bounds)
connection: Examples to check: number of prime factors-related counts, r(n) for sums of a prime and a square-free?, number of divisors in a dense set; the 'every n has ≫ log n representations as p + 2^a + 2^b' type (false). F04 + F21.
why: If no natural polylog-scale pointwise lower bound has ever been proved, ES's required statement is unprecedented — a strong strategic datum.
first_step: Ask MathOverflow-style search: 'every integer has at least log n representations'; check Erdős–Fuchs-type and additive-basis-order results.

title: Feature flip F35: problems where bounded certificate schemes DO work (Pratt certificates for primality) vs ES's B1
connection: Primality has short certificates (Pratt) found by structured search, but no bounded formula; ES has short certificates (F32) and B1 forbids bounded procedures under Schinzel H.
why: Pratt-style recursive certificates (certificate for p uses certificates for factors of p−1) suggest recursive ES certificates using solutions for factors of 4Cp+1 or p+4d.
first_step: Check whether an ES solution for p can be assembled from ES-like data for prime factors of 4Cp+1 (recursive certificate).

title: Feature flip F26: ES over F_q[T] (proved variants) vs. ℤ — the missing Weil-type pointwise bound
connection: In F_q[T], pointwise character-sum bounds (Weil/Deligne) are available at a single modulus; over ℤ only Burgess-type. That is the B2 gap.
why: Quantifies the exact deficit: what pointwise character-sum saving at modulus 4uB would make ES over ℤ follow.
first_step: Translate the F_q[T] proof into the needed ℤ-estimate and check whether it is implied by GLH or is stronger.

title: Gauss Eureka (n = Δ + Δ + Δ ⟺ 8n + 3 = sum of three odd squares): linear change of variable to a local-global problem
connection: ∀n statement solved by transforming n ↦ 8n + 3 and invoking three squares. ES's divisor forms also transform p ↦ 4Cp + 1, p + 4d (F10).
why: A single fixed affine transformation sufficed there; ES needs a family of transformations (one per C) — the cost of the extra quantifier.
first_step: Look for an ES equivalent with a single affine transform (e.g. a statement about 4p + 1 alone with a richer witness) — e.g. via the Frobenius semigroup item.

title: Waring's problem: G(3) and the finite exceptional sets (23, 239 need 9 cubes)
connection: ∀n statements with finite explicit exception lists (F25), proved via circle method + explicit computation; 'every large n is a sum of 4 cubes' open (count polylog-ish? no — n^{1/3}).
why: Sums of 4 cubes: almost-all known (Davenport), pointwise open, count ≍ n^{1/3} — a sibling for calibrating ES programs.
first_step: List which ES-program steps would, mutatis mutandis, prove 'every large n is a sum of 4 cubes' (calibration).

title: Schinzel–Sierpiński: every positive rational is (p+1)/(q+1)? — follows from Hypothesis H; ES's B1 uses H in the opposite direction
connection: Under Schinzel's H many ∀∃ prime statements hold; for ES, H implies every bounded procedure fails (B1 Thm C). Shares F35, F01.
why: Interesting duality: H supplies primes where we want them (for existence) and where we don't (to defeat finite procedures).
first_step: Ask whether H also implies ES (it supplies primes in polynomial families — could it supply divisors in classes?) — likely not, but record why.

title: Chen's theorem (p + 2 = P₂) and 'almost-ES' with a relaxed term
connection: Chen circumvented parity by allowing almost-primes. ES analogue: 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + a/z with a small, or with one denominator only 'almost integral' (z ∈ ½ℤ). Note numerator 2 makes ES trivial for p ≡ 1 mod 4 (4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 2/z).
why: Find the weakest relaxation that is not trivial — that marks where the parity-type barrier sits.
first_step: Check triviality for relaxations: (i) z ∈ ½ℤ, (ii) one denominator may be divisible by p², (iii) a/z with a = 3; record first nontrivial one.

title: Hardy–Littlewood conjecture F (primes of form n − k²) / Bateman–Horn: singular series with Legendre-symbol factors
connection: Representation counts with singular series involving (n/ℓ) — vanishing for squares-type n (e.g. n = k² + 1 issues). ES's main term M_BM has the same Legendre-symbol structure (F20).
why: Lets ES borrow the full Bateman–Horn singular-series machinery for its main term, and the known numerics for its variance.
first_step: Compare M_BM(p)/M₀(p) with a Bateman–Horn-type product ∏(1 − (p/ℓ)/(ℓ−1)) — is it asymptotically such a product?

title: Elliott–Halberstam-type level of distribution for divisor-in-class counts (Fouvry–Iwaniec, Friedlander–Iwaniec d₃)
connection: Distribution of τ-type functions in APs beyond √x is known for d₂ (Selberg/Hooley/Heath-Brown) and d₃ (Friedlander–Iwaniec, Fouvry–Kowalski–Michel). ES sums divisor-in-class counts over p-tied integers.
why: These give averages over moduli (B2); pointwise not. Still the best tools for the averaged ES problems (exceptional set).
first_step: Check whether the 3/4 exceptional-set barrier (F40) can be moved by a d₃-in-APs level beyond 1/2 input.
refs: unverified: Friedlander, Iwaniec 1985, Incomplete Kloosterman sums and a divisor problem (Annals)

title: OEIS search: numbers not of the form tuv − u − v (t,u,v ≥ 2) and with 4 | t — is the sequence in OEIS?
connection: U(n)'s failure set (odd squares + {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145}) is an explicit sequence; if it (or its variants) appears in OEIS, cross-references may reveal an independent characterisation.
why: OEIS cross-links occasionally reveal a known theorem behind a computed list.
first_step: Query OEIS for 105, 2961, 3985, 25305 and for the 14 (★) failure primes (409, …, 8813281).

title: OEIS A005097 (odd primes − 1)/2 ↔ numbers not of form 2xy + x + y: the bilinear primality template
connection: n ≠ 2xy + x + y ⟺ 2n + 1 prime: the simplest 'trilinear-word ⟺ primality' dictionary. ES's (★) word is the level-4C version with a sign flip.
why: These dictionaries show which word forms detect primality (dead) and which can be universal (ES) — the sign/level flip is the difference.
first_step: Generalise: for the form t·xy − x − y with fixed t, characterise non-represented n via divisors of tn + 1 ≡ −1 mod t; tabulate t = 2..12.
